name: UK Post-Punk
hook: Punk's DIY permission, pointed at dub, funk, and art-school ideas instead of at more punk.

blurb.age7: After punk, some bands used the same do-it-yourself attitude to make music that did not sound like punk at all.
blurb.age13: Once punk's initial burst was over, some of its musicians used the confidence it gave them, that anyone could start a band and make a record, to build something stranger. Public Image Ltd is the clearest case here: John Lydon left the Sex Pistols and, with a bassist who had learned from Jamaican sound systems, built songs almost entirely out of bass and space.
blurb.adult: Post-punk's real innovation is structural rather than stylistic: importing dub's logic of space, bass as the lead instrument, effects as compositional tools, directly into guitar music, rather than repeating punk's own new orthodoxy. London's multiracial working-class geography made that specific import, from Jamaican sound system culture rather than from any other available source, close to inevitable.

geopolitics: Late-1970s Britain combined high unemployment, industrial decline, and a resurgent far-right National Front active in London street politics. Rock Against Racism, formed in 1976, organized gigs deliberately pairing punk and post-punk acts with reggae acts as a direct response.
whatWasNew: Treating dub's structural logic, negative space, bass as the lead voice, effects as instruments, as available material for guitar-based rock, rather than repeating punk's own new orthodoxy.
production: A mix of larger independents like Virgin and smaller DIY labels, generally still modest budgets by mainstream rock standards but higher than punk's rushed early sessions.
labels: Virgin signed several of the scene's key acts directly; a wider network of small independent labels handled much of the rest.
politics: Broadly anti-racist and anti-establishment currents, shaped directly by Rock Against Racism and the National Front's street presence in the same period.
